images.title: Cut at the thirds: hexagon or octagon?
images.purpose: Compare cutting corners at the thirds: the triangle leaves a regular hexagon, the square leaves an octagon that is not regular.
images.composition: Two shapes side by side on white with no panel borders: a triangle on the left, a square on the right, each with its cut corners shown in grey.
images.exact_structure: Left: an equilateral triangle of side 9 cm, point up, each side marked into 3 equal parts of 3 cm. The 3 corner triangles (each equilateral, side 3 cm) are drawn with grey #6B7280 dashed outlines and no fill. The shape left is a hexagon filled green #009E73 with 6 equal sides, each with one small tick mark; one side carries the label '3 cm'. Under it, 'regular hexagon'. Right: a square of side 9 cm, drawn at the same scale as the triangle so every 3 cm side is the same length on screen, each side marked into 3 equal parts. The 4 corner right triangles (legs 3 cm and 3 cm) have grey dashed outlines and no fill. The shape left is an octagon filled vermilion #D55E00: its 4 straight sides (3 cm) carry one tick each and its 4 slanted sides carry two ticks each. One straight side is labelled '3 cm' and one slanted side 'about 4.24 cm'. Under it, 'not regular'.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
images.takeaway: Cutting at the thirds gives equal sides for a triangle but not for a square.

images.teaching_notes: '3 cm' appears once on each shape.

image_decisions.why: Equal and unequal sides are a visual fact; tick marks show it at a glance.
